records.content:
Features such as a color, a country, or a blood type take a finite number of categories and have no numeric meaning. If a column contains the codes 1, 2, 3 for three categories, a linear model would treat “3” as three times “1”, which is nonsense unless the categories are naturally ordered. Two encodings are standard.

Ordinal encoding maps ordered categories to integers (low < medium < high becomes 0, 1, 2). Use it only when the order is meaningful.

One-hot encoding creates one 0/1 column per category (the “dummy variables”): exactly one of them is 1 in each row. It makes no assumption about order.

The Diabetes data has no categorical column, so we create two, purely for demonstration: the sex column holds the codes 1 and 2 (their meaning is not documented in the data set, and we simply treat them as labels), and we cut age into three groups. The second is a loss of information, which we would not do in a real analysis, but it gives us an ordered categorical feature.

from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder, OrdinalEncoder

age_group = pd.cut(raw["age"], bins=[0, 40, 55, 100], labels=["young", "middle", "senior"])
print("people per age group:", age_group.value_counts().reindex(["young", "middle", "senior"]).to_dict())

onehot = OneHotEncoder(sparse_output=False).fit(age_group.to_frame())          # input: a DataFrame with one column
print("\none-hot columns:", list(onehot.get_feature_names_out()))
print("first 3 rows:\n", onehot.transform(age_group.to_frame())[:3])

ordinal = OrdinalEncoder(categories=[["young", "middle", "senior"]])             # we state the order explicitly
print("ordinal codes of the first 3 rows:", ordinal.fit_transform(age_group.to_frame())[:3].ravel())



The dummy-variable trap. The three one-hot columns always add up to 1, which is the same as the intercept column of ones. A linear model with an intercept and all three dummies has linearly dependent columns: this is exactly the situation of Exercise 1.10, in which \mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X} is singular. The remedy is to drop one category (OneHotEncoder(drop="first")): the dropped category becomes the reference level, absorbed by the intercept.

dummies = pd.get_dummies(age_group).to_numpy(dtype=float)                  # all three levels
design_all = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(dummies)), dummies])             # intercept + 3 dummies
design_drop = design_all[:, :3]                                            # intercept + 2 dummies
print(f"intercept + 3 dummies: shape {design_all.shape}, rank {np.linalg.matrix_rank(design_all)}  -> columns are dependent")
print(f"intercept + 2 dummies: shape {design_drop.shape}, rank {np.linalg.matrix_rank(design_drop)}  -> full column rank")



Two more practical points. A categorical column with thousands of categories (a postal code, a user identifier) cannot be one-hot encoded naively, because it creates thousands of columns; there are special techniques for such cases, which we will not need in this book. And when a category appears in the test set that was not in the training set, OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore") encodes it as a row of zeros instead of raising an error.

records.content:
We now assemble the pieces in one object. A ColumnTransformer applies different transformations to different groups of columns: numerical columns are scaled and imputed, categorical ones are one-hot encoded. A Pipeline chains this preprocessing with a model. The resulting object has the usual fit and predict methods, and fit learns everything (means, standard deviations, imputation values, categories, weights) from the training set only.

We use the Diabetes data with the two categorical columns of the previous section, with the same 10% of missing entries in the numerical columns, and a plain linear regression as the model. To judge the different treatments of the missing values fairly we repeat the experiment on 30 random 70/30 splits and report the mean and standard deviation of the R^2 on the test set; as a reference we also train on the original complete data.

from sklearn.base import clone
from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline

# Data frame with two categorical columns, complete and with the missing entries of the previous section
X_all = raw.drop(columns="target").copy()
y_diab = raw["target"]
X_all["sex"] = X_all["sex"].astype(int).astype(str)                       # the codes 1 and 2 as labels
X_all["age_group"] = age_group.astype(str)
cat_cols = ["sex", "age_group"]
X_holes = X_all.copy()
X_holes[num_cols] = X_holes[num_cols].mask(mask)                         # NaN where `mask` is True

def make_model(imputer):
    # Scale first (NaN are ignored when fitting and kept in the output), then impute on comparable scales
    numeric = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), imputer)
    prep = ColumnTransformer([("num", numeric, num_cols),
                              ("cat", OneHotEncoder(drop="first"), cat_cols)])
    return Pipeline([("prep", prep), ("regression", LinearRegression())])

print(make_model(SimpleImputer()))



def repeated_r2(X, y, build, seeds=range(30), drop_incomplete_rows=False):
    """Test R^2 of a pipeline over several random splits."""
    scores = []
    for seed in seeds:
        X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.3, random_state=seed)
        if drop_incomplete_rows:                                          # use only the complete training rows
            keep = ~X_tr[num_cols].isna().any(axis=1)
            X_tr, y_tr = X_tr[keep], y_tr[keep]
        scores.append(build().fit(X_tr, y_tr).score(X_te, y_te))
    return np.mean(scores), np.std(scores)

experiments = {
    "complete data (reference)":      (X_all,   lambda: make_model(SimpleImputer()),                False),
    "mean imputation":                (X_holes, lambda: make_model(SimpleImputer()),                False),
    "median imputation":              (X_holes, lambda: make_model(SimpleImputer(strategy="median")), False),
    "mean + missing indicators":      (X_holes, lambda: make_model(SimpleImputer(add_indicator=True)), False),
    "k-NN imputation (k = 5)":        (X_holes, lambda: make_model(KNNImputer(n_neighbors=5)),     False),
    "drop incomplete training rows":  (X_holes, lambda: make_model(SimpleImputer()),                True),
}
results = pd.DataFrame(
    [(name, *repeated_r2(X, y_diab, build, drop_incomplete_rows=drop)) for name, (X, build, drop) in experiments.items()],
    columns=["treatment of the missing values", "mean test R2", "std over splits"]).set_index("treatment of the missing values")
results.round(3)



# How many complete rows does the "drop" strategy have to train on? (the training set has 309 rows)
complete_in_train = [
    (~X_holes[num_cols].isna().any(axis=1).to_numpy()[train_test_split(np.arange(len(X_holes)), test_size=0.3, random_state=seed)[0]]).sum()
    for seed in range(30)
]
print(f"complete rows in a training set: {np.mean(complete_in_train):.0f} on average (out of 309)")



All treatments lose against the complete data, since the information is really gone, but they lose by very different amounts. Mean and median imputation cost about 0.045 of R^2; k-NN imputation recovers about half of that loss; adding missing-value indicators hurts here (nine more noisy columns for a training set of only 309 samples); and dropping incomplete rows is by far the worst, with an R^2 near 0.31 and a much larger variability between splits, because it trains on about 116 rows instead of 309. The ranking is a property of this data set and this model, but the lesson is general: do not throw data away if you can avoid it, and compare the treatments with the same protocol.

The whole procedure is a single object. We can inspect the names of the columns that the model receives, and apply it to new data with predict, without any manual step:

model = make_model(KNNImputer(n_neighbors=5))
X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(X_holes, y_diab, test_size=0.3, random_state=SEED)
model.fit(X_tr, y_tr)
print("features seen by the regression:", list(model.named_steps["prep"].get_feature_names_out()))
print("learned weights:", model.named_steps["regression"].coef_.round(2))
print("test R2 with this split:", round(model.score(X_te, y_te), 3))



Pitfall

Never call fit or fit_transform on the test set, and never preprocess the whole data set before splitting it. If you standardize X with StandardScaler().fit_transform(X) and only afterwards split into train and test, the mean and standard deviation of the test samples have influenced the training features. The effect is often small, but with imputers, feature selection, or target-dependent encodings it can be large, and it is invisible: your test score simply comes out better than the real performance. Put every learned step in a Pipeline and the problem cannot arise.

records.content:
Look at the data first: shapes, types, describe(), histograms, missing values (Sections 2.4 and 2.5).

Split before you fit anything; keep the test set untouched until the end.

Decide per column: numerical (scale, transform if skewed, impute), categorical (one-hot or ordinal), or to be discarded (identifiers, constant columns).

Wrap the steps in a ColumnTransformer and a Pipeline, so that fit uses the training data only and the very same transformations are applied at prediction time.

Compare alternatives with the same protocol, repeating over several splits when the data set is small.

Keep the raw data unchanged and write the preprocessing as code: it must be reproducible.

NumPy arrays have a shape and a dtype; slicing gives views, masks and fancy indexing give copies. axis=k is the axis that disappears in a reduction. Vectorize instead of looping, and use broadcasting (compare shapes from the right: equal or 1) with care: always check shapes, especially (n,) against (n, 1).

Numerical traps: do not compare floats with ==; avoid cancellation (use np.var); subtract the maximum before exponentiating (stable softmax); prefer log-probabilities to probabilities; solve systems with np.linalg.solve or lstsq, never with the explicit inverse; use eigh for symmetric matrices.

pandas DataFrames label the rows and columns: loc (labels, end included), iloc (positions), Boolean masks, groupby, describe, corr. Use .loc for assignments and .to_numpy() to get arrays.

Matplotlib: use fig, ax = plt.subplots() and the methods of the Axes. Honest figures have labeled axes, color-blind-safe colors with a second encoding, and show the spread.

Probability: Bayes’ rule \mathbb{P}(A\mid B) = \mathbb{P}(B\mid A)\mathbb{P}(A)/\mathbb{P}(B) (mind the prior!); \mathbb{E} is linear, \operatorname{Var}(X) = \mathbb{E}[X^2] - \mathbb{E}[X]^2; the covariance matrix \boldsymbol\Sigma is symmetric positive semidefinite, with eigenvectors that give the directions and eigenvalues that give the variances of the cloud; the multivariate Gaussian has elliptical level sets; the LLN and the CLT say that averages converge to the mean at rate 1/\sqrt{n} with Gaussian fluctuations.

Maximum likelihood maximizes \sum_i \log p(x_i;\theta): it gives \hat p = k/n for a Bernoulli and \hat\mu = \bar x, \hat\sigma^2 = \frac1n\sum(x_i-\bar x)^2 for a Gaussian. Least squares is maximum likelihood under Gaussian noise: a loss encodes a noise model.

Preprocessing: scale features (standardization by default), transform skewed ones, treat outliers with care, impute rather than drop, encode categories (one-hot, dropping one level when there is an intercept), and put everything in a Pipeline that is fitted on the training data only.

Iris: R. A. Fisher, “The use of multiple measurements in taxonomic problems”, Annals of Eugenics 7(2), 179–188 (1936). Bundled with scikit-learn.

Wine: M. Forina et al., PARVUS: An Extendible Package for Data Exploration, Classification and Correlation, Institute of Pharmaceutical and Food Analysis and Technologies, Genoa (1991). Obtained from the UCI Machine Learning Repository and bundled with scikit-learn.

Diabetes: B. Efron, T. Hastie, I. Johnstone and R. Tibshirani, “Least Angle Regression”, Annals of Statistics (with discussion), 407–499 (2004). Bundled with scikit-learn. The missing values and the categorical columns used in Section 2.7 were created artificially from the complete data, as explained there.

Breast Cancer Wisconsin (Diagnostic): W. N. Street, W. H. Wolberg and O. L. Mangasarian, “Nuclear feature extraction for breast tumor diagnosis”, IS&T/SPIE 1993 International Symposium on Electronic Imaging: Science and Technology, volume 1905, 861–870 (1993). Bundled with scikit-learn.

The screening-test numbers of Worked example 2.3 are illustrative.

C. R. Harris et al., “Array programming with NumPy”, Nature 585, 357–362 (2020).

W. McKinney, Python for Data Analysis, 3rd ed., O’Reilly, 2022 (pandas and NumPy in depth, by the author of pandas).

J. D. Hunter, “Matplotlib: A 2D graphics environment”, Computing in Science & Engineering 9(3), 90–95 (2007).

L. Wasserman, All of Statistics, Springer, 2004 (probability and maximum likelihood, concise and rigorous).

D. P. Bertsekas and J. N. Tsitsiklis, Introduction to Probability, 2nd ed., Athena Scientific, 2008 (Bayes’ rule, random variables, limit theorems).

R. J. A. Little and D. B. Rubin, Statistical Analysis with Missing Data, 3rd ed., Wiley, 2019 (MCAR, MAR, MNAR).

Difficulty: ★ warm-up, ★★ core, ★★★ challenge. Try each exercise before reading the hint; solutions and detailed outlines are in 

Appendix C.

Exercise 2.1 ★ — Shapes and broadcasting. Let A have shape (5, 3), v shape (3,), c shape (5, 1) and r shape (1, 3). (a) For each of the following expressions say whether it is valid and, if so, what its shape is: A + v, A + c, v + c, A @ v, A @ c, c @ r, r @ A. (b) Given X of shape (n, d), w of shape (d,) and y of shape (n,), write the mean squared error of the linear model in one NumPy expression and give the shape of every intermediate result. (c) If y has shape (n,) and y_hat has shape (n, 1), what is the shape of y - y_hat, and what number does np.mean((y - y_hat) ** 2) compute? Check your answer on the data of the Pitfall in Section 2.3.6.

Hint for (c). The result contains the entry (y_i - \hat y_j)^2 for every pair (i, j). Expand the square and average over i and j.

Exercise 2.2 ★ — Counting heads. Let X be the number of heads in three flips of a fair coin. (a) Write the probability mass function of X. (b) Compute \mathbb{E}[X] and \operatorname{Var}(X) from the definitions, and check them against the formulas np and np(1-p). (c) Let Z = 2X - 3. Compute \mathbb{E}[Z] and \operatorname{Var}(Z). What does Z represent?

Hint. The pmf of a Binomial(3, \tfrac12) is \binom{3}{k}/8. For (c) use \mathbb{E}[aX + b] = a\,\mathbb{E}[X] + b and \operatorname{Var}(aX + b) = a^2\operatorname{Var}(X).

Exercise 2.3 ★★ — A spam filter by Bayes. 40% of the e-mails that arrive are spam. The word “free” appears in 60% of the spam e-mails and in 5% of the legitimate ones (“ham”). (a) What is the probability that an e-mail is spam, given that it contains “free”? (b) The word “winner” appears in 30% of the spam and in 2% of the ham. Assuming that, within each class, the two words occur independently, what is the probability that an e-mail containing both words is spam? (c) Which assumption did you use in (b), and what can go wrong if it is false?

Hint. Use Bayes’ rule with the law of total probability in the denominator, as in Worked example 2.3. For (b), multiply the likelihoods of the two words inside each class.

Exercise 2.4 ★★ — Maximum likelihood for the exponential distribution. Let x_1, \dots, x_n be independent draws from the exponential distribution with density f(x;\lambda) = \lambda e^{-\lambda x} for x \ge 0. (a) Write the log-likelihood \ell(\lambda) and find the maximum likelihood estimate \hat\lambda. (b) Verify with the second derivative that it is a maximum. (c) Compute \hat\lambda for the data 0.5,\ 1.5,\ 1.0,\ 2.0, and say what the mean of the fitted distribution is.

Hint. \log f(x_i;\lambda) = \log\lambda - \lambda x_i. The mean of the exponential distribution is 1/\lambda (see the table in Section 2.6.4).

Exercise 2.5 ★★★ — Covariance matrices and whitening. Let \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^2 be a random vector with \mathbb{E}[\mathbf{x}] = \mathbf{0} and covariance matrix \boldsymbol{\Sigma} = \begin{pmatrix} 5 & 2 \\ 2 & 2 \end{pmatrix}. (a) Find the eigenvalues and orthonormal eigenvectors of \boldsymbol{\Sigma}. What are the variances of \mathbf{x} along those two directions? (b) Prove that for any matrix \mathbf{A}, the vector \mathbf{z} = \mathbf{A}\mathbf{x} has covariance \mathbf{A}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\mathbf{A}^\top, and that \boldsymbol{\Sigma} is positive semidefinite. (c) Find a matrix \mathbf{A} such that \operatorname{Cov}(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{I} (a whitening transformation) and verify it. (d) If \mathbf{x} is Gaussian, what is the probability that \mathbf{x}^\top\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\mathbf{x} \le 4?

Hint. For (b), \operatorname{Cov}(\mathbf{z}) = \mathbb{E}[\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}\mathbf{x}^\top\mathbf{A}^\top] and \mathbf{v}^\top\boldsymbol\Sigma\mathbf{v} = \operatorname{Var}(\mathbf{v}^\top\mathbf{x}). For (c), write \boldsymbol\Sigma = \mathbf{Q}\boldsymbol\Lambda\mathbf{Q}^\top and try \mathbf{A} = \boldsymbol\Lambda^{-1/2}\mathbf{Q}^\top. For (d), use the formula of Section 2.6.5.

Exercise 2.6 ★ — Array warm-up on Iris. (a) Compute the mean of each of the four features for each of the three species with a Boolean mask and a loop over the species, and check the result against pandas’ groupby. (b) Standardize the columns of the Iris data matrix with broadcasting (no scikit-learn) and verify that the means are 0 and the standard deviations 1. (c) Show that the covariance matrix of the standardized data (computed with ddof=0) is equal to the correlation matrix of the original data.

Hint. np.cov(Z, rowvar=False, ddof=0) and np.corrcoef(X, rowvar=False). Why does standardizing turn covariances into correlations?

Exercise 2.7 ★★ — A k-NN classifier without loops over the samples. Write a function knn_predict(X_train, y_train, X_test, k) that returns the predicted labels for the rows of X_test, using the Gram-matrix identity of Worked example 2.1 to compute all distances at once, np.argpartition (or np.argsort) to find the k nearest neighbors, and a majority vote. Test it on the standardized Wine data, with 30 random stratified 70/30 splits and k = 5, and compare the predictions with those of KNeighborsClassifier. How often do they agree? What is the mean test accuracy?

Hint. The distances from the test points to the training points form a matrix of shape (n_test, n_train). For the vote you may loop over the test points, or use np.apply_along_axis with np.bincount(...).argmax().

Exercise 2.8 ★★ — Exploring the Breast Cancer data with pandas. Load the Breast Cancer Wisconsin data with load_breast_cancer(as_frame=True). (a) How many samples are there in each class, and what do 0 and 1 mean? (b) For each of the 30 features compute the standardized difference between the classes, d_j = \lvert \bar x_{j,0} - \bar x_{j,1}\rvert / s_{p,j}, where s_{p,j} is the pooled standard deviation, s_p^2 = \frac{(n_0 - 1)s_0^2 + (n_1 - 1)s_1^2}{n_0 + n_1 - 2}. Which five features separate the classes best, and which three worst? (c) Draw a scatter plot of the two best features, with different colors and markers per class. (d) Compute the correlation between mean radius and mean perimeter and comment: what does it suggest about using both features in a linear model?

Hint. df.groupby("target").mean(), Series.sort_values(). A large d_j means that the class means are far apart compared with the spread inside a class.

Exercise 2.9 ★★★ — How fast is the central limit theorem? Repeat the experiment of Section 2.6.6 for the uniform distribution on [0, 1] (mean 1/2, variance 1/12) with 200,000 repetitions. For n = 1, 2, 3, 5, 10, compute the Kolmogorov-Smirnov distance between the standardized sample mean and the standard Gaussian, and plot it against n on a log-log scale together with the same quantity for the exponential distribution. Estimate the slope of each curve with np.polyfit on the logarithms. Which distribution converges faster, and why? (Hint: compare the skewness of the two distributions.)

Hint. Standardized mean: \sqrt{n}\,(\bar X_n - \mu)/\sigma with \sigma = \sqrt{1/12}. For the exponential with \lambda = 1 the skewness is 2 and for the uniform it is 0. A theory of the error terms (Edgeworth expansions) says that the leading error is proportional to the skewness divided by \sqrt{n}.

Exercise 2.10 ★★★ — A preprocessing laboratory, and a leak. (a) On the Wine data, compare no scaling, standardization, min-max scaling and robust scaling for k-NN with k \in \{1, 5, 15\}, with 30 stratified 70/30 splits, and present the mean test accuracies in a table. (b) Now commit the error of Section 2.7 on purpose: standardize the whole data set first, then split. Compare, for the same splits, with the correct pipeline. Is the difference systematic? (c) Leakage is much more dangerous when the preprocessing step uses the labels. Generate n = 60 samples of 2000 independent Gaussian features and random labels (so that there is nothing to learn), and repeat 30 times: select the 10 features with the highest f_classif score (SelectKBest) on the whole data set, then split, fit 5-NN, and compute the test accuracy. Compare with the correct procedure, in which the selection is part of a Pipeline fitted on the training set only. What accuracy should one expect on pure noise, and what do you observe?

Hint. For (a) and (b) reuse the function knn_accuracy of Section 2.7.1 in a modified form. For (c): SelectKBest(f_classif, k=10), make_pipeline(SelectKBest(...), KNeighborsClassifier(5)).

In Chapter 3 we turn the informal ideas of Chapter 1 (expected risk, empirical risk, generalization) into a precise theory, using the probability of this chapter: the expectation and the law of large numbers will be the main tools. From Chapter 4 on, we study learning methods one at a time. We begin with the simplest one, k-nearest neighbors, which you already know how to implement with the vectorized distances of this chapter, and we use it to understand the central trade-off between bias and variance.
Why does a model that fits the training data also work on new data? When can we trust it, and how much?

records.content:
Everything in this chapter rests on one modeling assumption. There is a joint distribution \mathcal{D} over pairs (\mathbf{x}, y) of an input and a label, which we cannot see, and the training setS = \{(\mathbf{x}_1, y_1), \dots, (\mathbf{x}_n, y_n)\}

consists of n pairs drawn independently from \mathcal{D} (“i.i.d.”: independent and identically distributed). A future example, the one we care about, is one more independent draw from the same \mathcal{D}. A prediction function is a map f from inputs to predictions \hat y = f(\mathbf{x}), and a loss \ell(y, \hat y) \ge 0 scores a single prediction (Section 1.5). The two quantities that matter areR(f) = \mathbb{E}_{(\mathbf{x}, y) \sim \mathcal{D}}\big[\ell\big(y, f(\mathbf{x})\big)\big]
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\hat{R}_S(f) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} \ell\big(y_i, f(\mathbf{x}_i)\big).

R(f) is the expected risk (also called the true risk or the generalization error): the average loss on a new example. \hat{R}_S(f) is the empirical risk: the average loss on the training set, which we can compute. The first is what we want; the second is what we have. Section 2.6 told us that \hat{R}_S(f) is a sample mean of the random variable \ell(y, f(\mathbf{x})) and that R(f) is its expectation, so the whole chapter is about how far a sample mean can be from the mean when the function f itself has been chosen by looking at the sample.

Pitfall — the i.i.d. assumption is a modeling choice, not a fact

The theory below applies when the training examples are independent draws and the future examples come from the same distribution. It fails, quietly, when the data are a time series (today resembles yesterday), when several rows come from the same patient or the same house (they are not independent), or when the model will be used on a different population from the one it was trained on. These situations do not make learning impossible, but the guarantees of this chapter no longer apply as stated, and the splitting strategy has to change (Chapter 5). Most “my model worked in the lab and failed in production” stories are violations of this assumption.

hierarchy.lvl3: 3.2.2 The best possible predictor: the Bayes predictor
hierarchy.lvl2: 3.2 The setting: distribution, loss, and risk

records.content:
If we knew \mathcal{D}, which function would we choose? Take the infimum of the risk over all functions,R^\ast = \inf_{f} R(f),

and call a function that achieves it a Bayes-optimal predictor f^\ast. It is a benchmark that no method, however clever and however much data it has, can beat. It can be found one input at a time, because the risk is an average over \mathbf{x} of a conditional risk:R(f) = \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x}}\Big[\,\underbrace{\mathbb{E}\big[\ell(y, f(\mathbf{x})) \mid \mathbf{x}\big]}_{\text{conditional risk at } \mathbf{x}}\,\Big].

This is the law of total expectation of Section 2.6. To make R(f) small it is enough, and necessary, to make the conditional risk small at every \mathbf{x}, which means choosing for each \mathbf{x} the best single prediction a = f(\mathbf{x}) given what \mathbf{x} tells us about y. Let us do it for the two most common losses.

Squared loss (regression). Write \eta(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbb{E}[y \mid \mathbf{x}], the conditional mean. For any number a,\mathbb{E}\big[(y - a)^2 \mid \mathbf{x}\big]
= \mathbb{E}\big[(y - \eta(\mathbf{x}))^2 \mid \mathbf{x}\big] + (\eta(\mathbf{x}) - a)^2
= \operatorname{Var}(y \mid \mathbf{x}) + (\eta(\mathbf{x}) - a)^2 .

(Add and subtract \eta(\mathbf{x}) inside the square; the cross term has zero expectation because \mathbb{E}[y - \eta(\mathbf{x}) \mid \mathbf{x}] = 0.) The second term is smallest, and equal to zero, for a = \eta(\mathbf{x}). Hence\boxed{\,f^\ast(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbb{E}[y \mid \mathbf{x}], \qquad R^\ast = \mathbb{E}\big[\operatorname{Var}(y \mid \mathbf{x})\big]\,}
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
R(f) - R^\ast = \mathbb{E}\big[(f(\mathbf{x}) - \eta(\mathbf{x}))^2\big].

The best regression function is the conditional mean, and the floor R^\ast is the average noise around it: the part of y that the input does not determine. For a constant predictor (no input) this is the result of Section 1.5, the sample mean; for the Bayes predictor the same idea is applied at every \mathbf{x}.

0–1 loss (binary classification). Let y \in \{0, 1\} and \eta(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbb{P}(y = 1 \mid \mathbf{x}). Predicting a \in \{0, 1\} is wrong with probability \mathbb{P}(y \neq a \mid \mathbf{x}), which is 1 - \eta(\mathbf{x}) if a = 1 and \eta(\mathbf{x}) if a = 0. The smaller of the two is obtained by predicting the more probable class:\boxed{\,f^\ast(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbb{I}\big[\eta(\mathbf{x}) > \tfrac12\big], \qquad R^\ast = \mathbb{E}\big[\min\{\eta(\mathbf{x}),\, 1 - \eta(\mathbf{x})\}\big]\,}

This is the Bayes classifier. By Bayes’ rule of Section 2.6 it can be written in terms of the class-conditional densities p_k(\mathbf{x}) and the priors \pi_k = \mathbb{P}(y = k): predict class 1 when \pi_1 p_1(\mathbf{x}) > \pi_0 p_0(\mathbf{x}). The floor R^\ast is the average, over \mathbf{x}, of the probability of the less likely class: it is zero only if the label is a deterministic function of the input.

(For the absolute loss \lvert y - a \rvert the same argument gives the conditional median instead of the mean; see Exercise 3.2.)

Key idea

Noise sets a floor. Even a perfect learner with infinite data has an error R^\ast > 0 whenever the label is not a function of the features alone. Two patients with identical measurements can have different outcomes; two e-mails with identical words can be spam and not spam. A model with 85% accuracy on a problem whose Bayes accuracy is 86% is excellent; the same model on a problem whose Bayes accuracy is 99% is poor. On real data R^\ast is unknown, which is why a single accuracy number can never tell whether there is room for improvement.

hierarchy.lvl2: 3.2 The setting: distribution, loss, and risk

records.content:
Let the input be a single number x and the two classes be equally likely, with x \mid y = 0 \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1) and x \mid y = 1 \sim \mathcal{N}(3, 1). With equal priors the Bayes classifier predicts the class with the larger density; the two Gaussians have the same variance, so their densities are equal at the midpoint, andf^\ast(x) = \mathbb{I}[x > 1.5].

An error occurs when a class-0 point falls to the right of 1.5 or a class-1 point falls to the left of it. By symmetry both events have the same probability, \mathbb{P}(\mathcal{N}(0, 1) > 1.5) = \Phi(-1.5), where \Phi is the cumulative distribution function of the standard Gaussian. HenceR^\ast = \tfrac12\,\Phi(-1.5) + \tfrac12\,\Phi(-1.5) = \Phi(-1.5) \approx 0.0668 .

Even in this friendly problem, 6.7% of the examples are misclassified by the best possible rule, because the two bells overlap. Let us check the number with a simulation.

rng = np.random.default_rng(SEED)
n_mc = 1_000_000
y = rng.integers(0, 2, size=n_mc)                       # equally likely classes
x = rng.normal(loc=3.0 * y, scale=1.0)                  # class 0: N(0,1), class 1: N(3,1)

bayes_pred = (x > 1.5).astype(int)
print(f"exact Bayes risk  Phi(-1.5)      : {stats.norm.cdf(-1.5):.4f}")
print(f"Monte Carlo risk of the rule x>1.5: {np.mean(bayes_pred != y):.4f}")
for t in (1.0, 1.25, 1.75, 2.0):                        # any other threshold does worse
    print(f"risk of the rule x>{t:<4}          : {np.mean((x > t) != y):.4f}")

records.content:
For the experiments of this chapter we need a problem in the plane where the Bayes classifier is known, but where a linear classifier cannot reach it. Class 0 is a round Gaussian cloud centered at the origin. Class 1 is a narrow vertical band: a Gaussian with a small variance in x_1 and a large variance in x_2, centered at (0.6, 0). The classes are equally likely. We will call it the simulated world.

The log-ratio of two Gaussian densities is a quadratic function of \mathbf{x}, so the boundary of the Bayes classifier is a conic (here two curves), not a line. That is deliberate: it will let us see, in numbers, the difference between the best that any classifier can do and the best that a linear classifier can do.

from scipy.stats import multivariate_normal

# The simulated world: two classes in the plane, equally likely.
MU = [np.array([0.0, 0.0]), np.array([0.6, 0.0])]
COV = [np.diag([1.0, 1.0]), np.diag([0.1, 6.0])]
dens = [multivariate_normal(MU[k], COV[k]) for k in (0, 1)]


def sample_world(n, rng):
    """Draw n i.i.d. pairs (x, y) from the distribution D of the simulated world."""
    y = rng.integers(0, 2, size=n)
    X = np.empty((n, 2))
    for k in (0, 1):
        idx = y == k
        X[idx] = rng.multivariate_normal(MU[k], COV[k], size=idx.sum())
    return X, y


def bayes_predict(X):
    """The Bayes classifier: predict the class with the larger density (the priors are equal)."""
    return (dens[1].logpdf(X) > dens[0].logpdf(X)).astype(int)


rng = np.random.default_rng(SEED)
X_big, y_big = sample_world(2_000_000, rng)
errors = bayes_predict(X_big) != y_big
R_BAYES = errors.mean()
print(f"Bayes risk R* of the simulated world: {R_BAYES:.4f}   (Monte Carlo error +/- {errors.std() / np.sqrt(len(errors)):.4f})")
print(f"error on class 0: {errors[y_big == 0].mean():.4f} | error on class 1: {errors[y_big == 1].mean():.4f}")



About 19% of the points are misclassified by the best possible rule: the Bayes risk of this world is R^\ast \approx 0.189. The next cell finds the best linear classifier of this world by brute force (all directions, all thresholds, on 300,000 points) and measures its risk on points it has not seen. The search is cheap because a linear classifier in the plane is a direction and a threshold.

def best_linear_classifier(X, y, n_angles=360):
    """Exhaustive search of the linear classifier with the smallest 0-1 error: 'predict 1 if w.x > t'."""
    n, best = len(y), (1.0, None, None)
    for theta in np.linspace(0, np.pi, n_angles, endpoint=False):
        w = np.array([np.cos(theta), np.sin(theta)])
        order = np.argsort(X @ w)
        ys, proj = y[order], (X @ w)[order]
        below1, below0 = np.cumsum(ys == 1), np.cumsum(ys == 0)
        err_pred1_above = below1 + (below0[-1] - below0)       # errors if we predict 1 above the cut after position i
        for sign, errs in ((1.0, err_pred1_above), (-1.0, n - err_pred1_above)):
            i = errs.argmin()
            if errs[i] / n < best[0]:
                cut = (proj[i] + proj[min(i + 1, n - 1)]) / 2
                best = (errs[i] / n, sign * w, sign * cut)
    return best


_, w_lin, t_lin = best_linear_classifier(X_big[:300_000], y_big[:300_000])
fresh = slice(300_000, None)                                      # points the search has never seen
R_LINEAR = np.mean((X_big[fresh] @ w_lin > t_lin).astype(int) != y_big[fresh])
print(f"best linear classifier: direction {np.round(w_lin, 3)}, threshold {t_lin:.3f}")
print(f"risk of the best linear classifier: {R_LINEAR:.4f}   (Bayes risk: {R_BAYES:.4f})")



The best linear classifier is a vertical line, with a risk of about 0.259: seven percentage points worse than the Bayes classifier, and no amount of data will close that gap, because the gap is a property of the class of functions, not of the sample. Figure 3.1 shows the two boundaries.

# Figure 3.1 — the simulated world: data, Bayes boundary, and the best linear boundary
def figure_3_1():
    rng = np.random.default_rng(SEED + 7)
    X, y = sample_world(500, rng)

    gx, gy = np.meshgrid(np.linspace(-3.6, 3.6, 400), np.linspace(-7.5, 7.5, 600))
    grid = np.column_stack([gx.ravel(), gy.ravel()])
    log_ratio = (dens[1].logpdf(grid) - dens[0].logpdf(grid)).reshape(gx.shape)

    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 6.6))
    ax.scatter(*X[y == 0].T, s=16, color=BLUE, marker="o", alpha=0.75, label="class 0")
    ax.scatter(*X[y == 1].T, s=18, color=ORANGE, marker="^", alpha=0.85, label="class 1")
    ax.contour(gx, gy, log_ratio, levels=[0], colors=[VERMILION], linewidths=2.2)
    ax.plot([], [], color=VERMILION, linewidth=2.2, label=f"Bayes boundary (risk {R_BAYES:.3f})")
    ax.axvline(t_lin, color="black", linestyle="--", linewidth=1.8, label=f"best linear boundary (risk {R_LINEAR:.3f})")
    ax.set(xlabel="$x_1$", ylabel="$x_2$", xlim=(-3.6, 3.6), ylim=(-7.5, 7.5),
           title="The simulated world and its two boundaries")
    ax.legend(loc="upper center", bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, -0.11), ncol=2, frameon=False, fontsize=9.5)
    fig.tight_layout()
    plt.show()


figure_3_1()



Class 0 (circles) is the round cloud. Class 1 (triangles) is the tall thin band that crosses it. The Bayes boundary (solid) has two branches, and class 1 is predicted between them: a region that is narrow near the origin and widens for large \lvert x_2 \rvert, where the broad class-1 density wins over the round class-0 density. No single straight line can do that. The best line (dashed) simply cuts the cloud vertically near x_1 \approx 0.1.

Try it

Change the covariance of class 1 in the cell that defines COV (for instance to np.diag([1.0, 1.0])) and re-run the notebook from that point on. With equal covariances the Bayes boundary becomes a straight line, the best linear classifier is the Bayes classifier, and the 7-point gap disappears.

hierarchy.lvl2: 3.3 Empirical risk minimization and the two sources of error
3.3 Empirical risk minimization and the two sources of error

records.content:
We cannot minimize R(f), because we do not know \mathcal{D}. We can minimize \hat{R}_S(f), which we can compute, and we cannot afford to search over all functions: with a finite sample, some function always matches the training labels exactly (for instance, a table of the training set, which says nothing about new inputs). So we restrict the search to a hypothesis class \mathcal{H}, a set of functions chosen in advance: the lines in the plane, the polynomials of degree at most 3, the neural networks with a given architecture. Empirical risk minimization returns a function of \mathcal{H} with the smallest empirical risk:\hat f_S \in \operatorname*{argmin}_{f \in \mathcal{H}} \hat{R}_S(f).

This is the principle announced in Section 1.5. Two remarks keep the story honest. First, \hat f_S depends on the random sample, so it is itself random: a different training set gives a different function. Second, for the 0–1 loss the minimization is computationally hard for many classes (minimizing the number of mistakes of a linear classifier is NP-hard in general), so practical methods minimize a smooth substitute such as the logistic loss (Chapter 6) or the hinge loss (Chapter 8). Here we think of ideal ERM, and in the experiments we use logistic regression as a practical stand-in.

hierarchy.lvl3: 3.3.1 The decomposition of the excess risk
hierarchy.lvl2: 3.3 Empirical risk minimization and the two sources of error

records.content:
Let f_{\mathcal{H}} be the best function in the class, f_{\mathcal{H}} \in \operatorname{argmin}_{f \in \mathcal{H}} R(f): the function we would pick if we knew \mathcal{D} but were limited to \mathcal{H}. Adding and subtracting R(f_{\mathcal{H}}) splits the excess risk of the learned function over the unbeatable Bayes risk into two parts:\underbrace{R(\hat f_S) - R^\ast}_{\text{excess risk}}
= \underbrace{\big[R(\hat f_S) - R(f_{\mathcal{H}})\big]}_{\text{estimation error}}
+ \underbrace{\big[R(f_{\mathcal{H}}) - R^\ast\big]}_{\text{approximation error}} .

The approximation error measures how well the class can do even with perfect knowledge of \mathcal{D}. It does not depend on n or on the sample; it shrinks only if we enlarge \mathcal{H}. In the simulated world, the approximation error of the lines is 0.259 - 0.189 = 0.070.

The estimation error measures what we lose by choosing the function from a finite random sample instead of from \mathcal{D}. It is random, it shrinks as n grows, and it grows with the richness of \mathcal{H} (more candidates, more ways to be fooled by the sample, as Section 3.4 shows).

Figure 3.2 sketches the picture: the Bayes predictor lives outside the class, the best function in the class is the closest we can get, and ERM lands somewhere around it.

# Figure 3.2 — a schematic of the two sources of error (not to scale)
def figure_3_2():
    from matplotlib.patches import Ellipse

    ax.plot(*p_best, marker="o", markersize=9, color=BLUE)
    ax.plot(*p_erm, marker="s", markersize=9, color=ORANGE)
    ax.annotate(r"Bayes predictor $f^*$" "\n" r"risk $R^*$", p_bayes, xytext=(1.5, 0.85), fontsize=10.5, ha="center", color=VERMILION)
    ax.annotate(r"best in class $f_{\mathcal{H}}$", p_best, xytext=(4.7, 1.0), fontsize=10.5, ha="center", color=BLUE)
    ax.annotate(r"ERM solution $\hat f_S$", p_erm, xytext=(8.0, 0.75), fontsize=10.5, ha="center", color="#8a5a00")

    ax.text(3.9, 2.62, "approximation\nerror", ha="center", fontsize=10)

hierarchy.lvl2: 3.3 Empirical risk minimization and the two sources of error
3.3 Empirical risk minimization and the two sources of error

records.content:
Enlarging \mathcal{H} reduces the approximation error and increases the estimation error. To see both effects we use classes of increasing richness: logistic regression on the polynomial features of degree m of (x_1, x_2), for m = 1 (lines), m = 2 (conics, which contain the Bayes classifier of this world, so the approximation error is zero), up to m = 8 (44 features). We draw many training sets of size n from the simulated world, fit each class, and measure the risk of the result on a fresh test set of 100,000 points, which gives the true risk up to a Monte Carlo error of about 0.001. We use a very weak regularization (C=1000) so that logistic regression behaves like unregularized ERM; the role of regularization is the subject of Chapter 6.

from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import PolynomialFeatures, StandardScaler


def make_poly_model(degree):
    return make_pipeline(PolynomialFeatures(degree, include_bias=False), StandardScaler(),
                         LogisticRegression(C=1000.0, max_iter=5000))


rng = np.random.default_rng(SEED + 1)
X_test, y_test = sample_world(100_000, rng)          # one big test set: its error is the true risk, up to ~0.001


def risks(degree, n, reps):
    """Mean training error and mean true risk of the fitted model, over `reps` training sets of size n."""
    train_err, test_err = [], []
    for _ in range(reps):
        X, y = sample_world(n, rng)
        model = make_poly_model(degree).fit(X, y)
        train_err.append(np.mean(model.predict(X) != y))
        test_err.append(np.mean(model.predict(X_test) != y_test))
    return np.mean(train_err), np.mean(test_err)


degrees = [1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8]
sizes_left = [30, 300, 3000]
by_degree = {n: [risks(m, n, reps=60) for m in degrees] for n in sizes_left}

table = pd.DataFrame({f"n={n}, test risk": [r[1] for r in by_degree[n]] for n in sizes_left}, index=degrees)
table["n=30, TRAINING error"] = [r[0] for r in by_degree[30]]
table.index.name = "degree m"
print(f"Bayes risk R* = {R_BAYES:.3f}; best linear classifier = {R_LINEAR:.3f}")
table.round(3)





Read the table column by column.

n = 30 (few data). The test risk is U-shaped: it falls from 0.34 (lines, large approximation error) to its minimum of 0.25 at degree 2, and then rises again to 0.30 at degree 8, because a class with 44 features has too much freedom for 30 points: the estimation error dominates. The training error (last column) does the opposite: it decreases all the way down to 0.05. The training error always prefers the richer class, and is therefore useless for choosing it.

n = 300. The best class is still degree 2, and the penalty for the richer classes has shrunk (0.207 at degree 8): more data, smaller estimation error.

n = 3000. Every class with degree \ge 2 is within noise of the Bayes risk (0.189): the estimation error has become negligible, and what separates the classes is only the approximation error, which is zero for all of them. The lines, instead, stay at 0.28 (the logistic loss is a proxy for the 0–1 loss, so it does a little worse than the best line, 0.259).

The second experiment shows the effect of n for three classes, in a learning curve.

sizes_curve = [10, 20, 40, 80, 160, 320, 640, 1280, 2560]
curve_degrees = [1, 2, 8]
curves = {m: [risks(m, n, reps=100 if n <= 320 else 40) for n in sizes_curve] for m in curve_degrees}
pd.DataFrame({f"degree {m}": [r[1] for r in curves[m]] for m in curve_degrees}, index=pd.Index(sizes_curve, name="n")).round(3)



# Figure 3.3 — approximation vs estimation error, measured in the simulated world
def figure_3_3():
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11.2, 4.4))

    ax = axes[0]
    styles = {30: (VERMILION, "o", "-"), 300: (BLUE, "s", "--"), 3000: (GREEN, "^", ":")}
    for n in sizes_left:
        color, marker, ls = styles[n]
        ax.plot(degrees, [r[1] for r in by_degree[n]], marker=marker, linestyle=ls, color=color, linewidth=2, label=f"test risk, n = {n}")
    ax.plot(degrees, [r[0] for r in by_degree[30]], marker="o", linestyle="-", color=VERMILION, alpha=0.4, label="training error, n = 30")
    ax.axhline(R_BAYES, color="black", linewidth=1.2)
    ax.text(8.1, R_BAYES - 0.012, "Bayes risk", ha="right", va="top", fontsize=9.5)
    ax.set(xlabel="degree $m$ of the polynomial features (richness of $\\mathcal{H}$)", ylabel="0-1 risk",
           title="(a) risk against richness, at fixed $n$")
    ax.set_ylim(0.03, 0.47)
    ax.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=9, ncol=2, loc="upper right")

    ax = axes[1]
    styles = {1: (VERMILION, "o", "-"), 2: (BLUE, "s", "--"), 8: (GREEN, "^", ":")}
    names = {1: "degree 1 (lines)", 2: "degree 2 (contains the Bayes classifier)", 8: "degree 8 (44 features)"}
    for m in curve_degrees:
        color, marker, ls = styles[m]
        ax.plot(sizes_curve, [r[1] for r in curves[m]], marker=marker, linestyle=ls, color=color, linewidth=2, label=names[m])
    ax.axhline(R_BAYES, color="black", linewidth=1.2)
    ax.axhline(R_LINEAR, color="gray", linewidth=1.2, linestyle="--")
    ax.text(10.5, R_BAYES + 0.004, "Bayes risk", va="bottom", fontsize=9.5)
    ax.text(2600, R_LINEAR + 0.004, "best line", va="bottom", ha="right", fontsize=9.5, color="gray")
    ax.set_xscale("log")
    ax.set(xlabel="training-set size $n$", ylabel="true risk", title="(b) learning curves")
    ax.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=9.5)
    fig.tight_layout()
    plt.show()


figure_3_3()



Panel (b) is the picture to remember. The lines (vermilion) flatten out high above the Bayes risk: more data will never help, because the approximation error is there to stay. Degree 2 (blue) converges to the Bayes risk quickly, since its class contains the Bayes classifier and has only 5 features. Degree 8 (green) also converges to the Bayes risk, since it contains degree 2, but it needs about four times more data to get there (it reaches a risk of 0.20 at n = 320, where degree 2 had it at n = 80): its extra freedom is a liability when n is small.

Key idea

The right complexity depends on the amount of data. With n = 30 the best class is small even if it is “wrong”; with n = 3000 any sufficiently rich class works. A fixed choice of model family is a bet on the amount of data and on the structure of the problem. The rest of Part II is about methods that adapt their complexity to the data: regularization (Chapter 6), margins (Chapter 8), pruning and ensembles (Chapter 11), and about choosing it by validation (Chapter 5), since the training error cannot do it, as the table has just shown. For the squared loss the same decomposition has a famous name, the bias–variance trade-off, studied in Chapter 4.

hierarchy.lvl2: 3.4 Why the training error is optimistic
3.4 Why the training error is optimistic

records.content:
Why does the training error of the richer classes keep falling while the test risk rises? There are two different statements to prove, and the difference between them is the heart of this chapter.

For a fixed function, the empirical risk is an honest estimate. Suppose f was chosen before seeing S (by a colleague, by a previous data set, by a coin). Then \ell(y_i, f(\mathbf{x}_i)) are i.i.d. random variables with mean R(f), and by the linearity of expectation\mathbb{E}_S\big[\hat{R}_S(f)\big] = \frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n \mathbb{E}\big[\ell(y_i, f(\mathbf{x}_i))\big] = R(f).

The empirical risk is an unbiased estimate of the true risk, and the law of large numbers (Section 2.6.6) says that it converges to it as n \to \infty. This is why a test set, used once on one function, can be trusted (Section 3.10).

For the function chosen by ERM it is not. The function \hat f_S is selected because it has a small empirical risk on this particular S. Using only the definition of ERM, \hat{R}_S(\hat f_S) \le \hat{R}_S(f_{\mathcal{H}}) for the best function in the class, and f_{\mathcal{H}} is a fixed function (it does not depend on S), so the previous paragraph applies to it:\mathbb{E}_S\big[\hat{R}_S(\hat f_S)\big] \;\le\; \mathbb{E}_S\big[\hat{R}_S(f_{\mathcal{H}})\big] \;=\; R(f_{\mathcal{H}}) \;\le\; \mathbb{E}_S\big[R(\hat f_S)\big].

The last inequality holds because R(f_{\mathcal{H}}) is the smallest risk in the class and \hat f_S belongs to the class. In words, on average, the training error of the ERM solution is below the best achievable risk in the class, which is below the true risk of the ERM solution. The training error is a biased, over-optimistic estimate, and the optimism is larger when the class is richer, as the table of Section 3.3 showed.

hierarchy.lvl2: 3.4 Why the training error is optimistic

hierarchy.lvl3: 3.4.1 Optimism grows with the number of candidates
hierarchy.lvl2: 3.4 Why the training error is optimistic

records.content:
How large can the optimism be? Take the most extreme situation: the labels are pure coin flips, so that every function has true risk exactly \tfrac12 and nothing can be learned. We try m candidate functions, so that each one predicts the n training labels at random and independently of the others (for instance, m random models, or m random subsets of features). The training error of each candidate is \text{Binomial}(n, \tfrac12)/n, and ERM keeps the smallest of the m values. Its expectation is computed exactly from the cumulative distribution of the binomial: since the minimum of m independent variables exceeds k - 1 with probability \big(\mathbb{P}(\text{Bin} \ge k)\big)^m,\mathbb{E}\Big[\min_{j \le m} \hat{R}_j\Big] = \frac1n \sum_{k=1}^{n} \big(1 - F(k-1)\big)^{m}, \qquad F = \text{cdf of } \text{Binomial}(n, \tfrac12).

def expected_min_error(n, m):
    """Exact expected smallest training error of m independent coin-flip classifiers, on n training points."""
    k = np.arange(1, n + 1)
    return np.sum((1 - stats.binom.cdf(k - 1, n, 0.5)) ** float(m)) / n


n = 50
rng = np.random.default_rng(SEED)
rows = []
for m in [1, 10, 100, 1_000, 10_000]:
    simulated = rng.binomial(n, 0.5, size=(2000, m)).min(axis=1).mean() / n      # brute force, 2000 repetitions
    rows.append((m, expected_min_error(n, m), simulated))
for m in [100_000, 1_000_000]:
    rows.append((m, expected_min_error(n, m), np.nan))
opt = pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=["candidates m", "expected best training error (exact)", "simulated"])
opt["true risk of every candidate"] = 0.5
print(opt.round(4).to_string(index=False))



With a single candidate the training error is 0.5, as it should. With a thousand candidates, the best one has a training error of about 0.27; with a million, about 0.17. All of these candidates are useless, with a true risk of exactly 0.5, and the best of them looks like a classifier with 83% accuracy. The simulation (third column) agrees with the exact formula. Figure 3.4 shows the optimism for several sample sizes, and compares it with the simple expression \sqrt{\ln m / (2n)} that we will prove in Section 3.6.

# Figure 3.4 — the optimism of the best of m useless candidates
def figure_3_4():
    ms = np.unique(np.logspace(0, 6, 40).astype(int))
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.6, 4.2))
    styles = {25: (VERMILION, "-"), 50: (BLUE, "--"), 100: (GREEN, "-."), 400: (PURPLE, ":")}
    for n_, (color, ls) in styles.items():
        gap = [0.5 - expected_min_error(n_, m) for m in ms]
        ax.plot(ms, gap, color=color, linestyle=ls, linewidth=2, label=f"exact optimism, $n$ = {n_}")
        ax.plot(ms, np.sqrt(np.log(ms) / (2 * n_)), color=color, linestyle=ls, linewidth=0.9, alpha=0.55)
    ax.plot([], [], color="gray", linewidth=0.9, label=r"$\sqrt{\ln m/(2n)}$ (thin lines)")
    ax.set_xscale("log")
    ax.set(xlabel="number of candidates $m$", ylabel="true risk minus best training error",
           title="Optimism of the best of $m$ useless candidates")
    ax.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=9.5)
    fig.tight_layout()
    plt.show()


figure_3_4()



Two facts stand out. The optimism grows with the logarithm of the number of candidates (going from a hundred to a million candidates only doubles it), and it shrinks like 1/\sqrt{n} when the sample grows. That is the pattern of the theory we are about to develop, and it matches the thin curves of the formula \sqrt{\ln m/(2n)}, which will turn out to be an upper bound on this optimism that is nearly attained here.

Pitfall — the winner’s curse

Every time you compare many models, many hyperparameter values or many feature subsets on the same data and keep the best one, you are doing what the experiment above does with m coin-flip classifiers: the winner’s score is optimistic, and more so the more you tried. This is exactly the leakage of Section 2.7 (feature selection on the whole data set gave 82% accuracy on pure noise), seen from the theory side. The cure is also the same: keep data that played no role in the selection, a validation set or a test set, to measure the winner (Chapter 5).

hierarchy.lvl2: 3.5 Concentration: from the law of large numbers to Hoeffding’s inequality
3.5 Concentration: from the law of large numbers to Hoeffding’s inequality

records.content: The law of large numbers says that the empirical risk of a fixed function converges to its true risk, but it does not say how fast, and a guarantee that “eventually” holds is of little use for a data set of 500 examples. We need a statement of the form “with probability at least 1 - \delta, the empirical risk is within \varepsilon of the true one, as soon as n is at least ...”. Such statements are called concentration inequalities. We build them in three steps, from the crudest to the sharpest.

hierarchy.lvl2: 3.5 Concentration: from the law of large numbers to Hoeffding’s inequality
3.5 Concentration: from the law of large numbers to Hoeffding’s inequality

records.content:
Markov’s inequality. If Z \ge 0 is a random variable and t > 0, then\mathbb{P}(Z \ge t) \le \frac{\mathbb{E}[Z]}{t}.

Proof. Z \ge t\,\mathbb{I}[Z \ge t] holds for every outcome, since Z \ge 0. Take expectations: \mathbb{E}[Z] \ge t\,\mathbb{P}(Z \ge t). \square

Applied to (Z - \mathbb{E}[Z])^2 it gives Chebyshev’s inequality, \mathbb{P}(\lvert Z - \mathbb{E}[Z]\rvert \ge t) \le \operatorname{Var}(Z)/t^2. For the mean \bar X_n of n independent variables with mean \mu and variance \sigma^2, whose variance is \sigma^2/n (Section 2.6.2),\mathbb{P}\big(\lvert \bar X_n - \mu\rvert \ge \varepsilon\big) \le \frac{\sigma^2}{n\varepsilon^2}.

This is already a non-asymptotic statement, but the probability decays only like 1/n: to be 99% sure we need a hundred times more data than to be 0% sure of nothing. We can do much better if the variables are bounded, as the losses of a classifier are.

hierarchy.lvl3: 3.5.2 The Chernoff method and Hoeffding’s inequality
hierarchy.lvl2: 3.5 Concentration: from the law of large numbers to Hoeffding’s inequality

hierarchy.lvl3: 3.5.2 The Chernoff method and Hoeffding’s inequality
hierarchy.lvl2: 3.5 Concentration: from the law of large numbers to Hoeffding’s inequality

records.content:
The idea of Chernoff is to apply Markov’s inequality not to Z but to e^{sZ}, for a free parameter s > 0 that we choose at the end: since z \mapsto e^{sz} is increasing,\mathbb{P}(Z \ge t) = \mathbb{P}\big(e^{sZ} \ge e^{st}\big) \le e^{-st}\,\mathbb{E}\big[e^{sZ}\big].

For a sum of independent variables, \mathbb{E}[e^{s\sum_i Z_i}] = \prod_i \mathbb{E}[e^{sZ_i}] factorizes, and what remains is to bound the moment generating function \mathbb{E}[e^{sZ_i}] of each term. For a bounded variable this is done by Hoeffding’s lemma.

Hoeffding’s lemma. If \mathbb{E}[X] = 0 and a \le X \le b, then for every s \in \mathbb{R}\mathbb{E}\big[e^{sX}\big] \le \exp\Big(\frac{s^2 (b - a)^2}{8}\Big).

Proof of Hoeffding’s lemma (you may skip it)

Since e^{sx} is a convex function of x, on the interval [a, b] it lies below its chord: e^{sx} \le \frac{b - x}{b - a} e^{sa} + \frac{x - a}{b - a} e^{sb}. Taking expectations and using \mathbb{E}[X] = 0 (note that a \le 0 \le b),\mathbb{E}\big[e^{sX}\big] \le \frac{b}{b - a}\,e^{sa} - \frac{a}{b - a}\,e^{sb}.

Let p = -a/(b - a) \in [0, 1] and u = s(b - a). Then b/(b - a) = 1 - p and sa = -pu, so the right-hand side equals e^{\varphi(u)} with\varphi(u) = -pu + \ln\big(1 - p + p\,e^{u}\big).

Differentiate: \varphi(0) = 0, \varphi'(u) = -p + \dfrac{p\,e^u}{1 - p + p\,e^u}, so \varphi'(0) = 0, and\varphi''(u) = q(1 - q) \quad\text{with}\quad q = \frac{p\,e^u}{1 - p + p\,e^u} \in [0, 1],

hence \varphi''(u) \le \tfrac14 for all u (the maximum of q(1-q) is \tfrac14). Taylor’s theorem with the remainder gives \varphi(u) = \varphi(0) + \varphi'(0)u + \tfrac12\varphi''(\xi)u^2 \le u^2/8 for some \xi between 0 and u. Therefore \mathbb{E}[e^{sX}] \le e^{u^2/8} = e^{s^2(b-a)^2/8}. \square

Hoeffding’s inequality. Let X_1, \dots, X_n be independent with X_i \in [a_i, b_i], and S_n = \sum_{i} X_i. Then for every t > 0\mathbb{P}\big(S_n - \mathbb{E}[S_n] \ge t\big) \le \exp\Big(-\frac{2t^2}{\sum_{i}(b_i - a_i)^2}\Big),

and the same bound holds for the lower tail. In particular, for the mean of n independent variables with values in [0, 1] and expectation \mu,\mathbb{P}\big(\bar X_n - \mu \ge \varepsilon\big) \le e^{-2n\varepsilon^2}, \qquad
\mathbb{P}\big(\lvert \bar X_n - \mu\rvert \ge \varepsilon\big) \le 2\,e^{-2n\varepsilon^2}.

Proof of Hoeffding’s inequality (you may skip it)

Apply the Chernoff method to S_n - \mathbb{E}[S_n] = \sum_i (X_i - \mathbb{E}[X_i]), whose terms are independent, have mean zero, and lie in an interval of length b_i - a_i. For any s > 0, by Markov’s inequality, independence, and Hoeffding’s lemma,\mathbb{P}\big(S_n - \mathbb{E}[S_n] \ge t\big) \le e^{-st}\prod_{i=1}^n \mathbb{E}\big[e^{s(X_i - \mathbb{E}X_i)}\big] \le \exp\Big(-st + \frac{s^2}{8}\sum_{i}(b_i - a_i)^2\Big).

The exponent is a quadratic function of s, minimized at s = 4t / \sum_i (b_i - a_i)^2, where it equals -2t^2/\sum_i (b_i - a_i)^2. For the mean, take t = n\varepsilon and \sum_i (b_i - a_i)^2 = n: the bound becomes \exp(-2n^2\varepsilon^2/n) = e^{-2n\varepsilon^2}. The two-sided bound adds the two tails. \square

From the inequality to a guarantee. Fix a function f before seeing the data, and let the loss be bounded in [0, 1] (as the 0–1 loss is). The numbers \ell(y_i, f(\mathbf{x}_i)) are i.i.d. with values in [0, 1] and mean R(f), so\mathbb{P}\big(\lvert \hat{R}_S(f) - R(f)\rvert \ge \varepsilon\big) \le 2\,e^{-2n\varepsilon^2}.

Setting the right-hand side equal to \delta and solving for \varepsilon gives the equivalent confidence form: with probability at least 1 - \delta over the draw of S,\boxed{\ \lvert \hat{R}_S(f) - R(f)\rvert \le \sqrt{\frac{\ln(2/\delta)}{2n}}\ }

The deviation shrinks like 1/\sqrt{n} and grows only like \sqrt{\ln(1/\delta)} when we ask for more confidence: being very sure is cheap, being very precise is expensive.

3.5 Concentration: from the law of large numbers to Hoeffding’s inequality

records.content:
Let us compare the bounds with the truth in a case where the truth can be computed exactly: the mean of n Bernoulli(0.3) variables, and the probability that it deviates from 0.3 by at least \varepsilon = 0.1. The exact probability comes from the binomial distribution; we also show the Gaussian approximation of the central limit theorem (Section 2.6.6), which is accurate but is not a guarantee.

p_true, eps = 0.3, 0.1


def exact_tail(n):
    """P(|mean - p| >= eps) for the mean of n Bernoulli(p) variables, from the binomial distribution."""
    lo = np.floor(n * (p_true - eps) + 1e-9)             # k/n <= p - eps   <=>   k <= lo
    hi = np.ceil(n * (p_true + eps) - 1e-9)              # k/n >= p + eps   <=>   k >= hi
    return stats.binom.cdf(lo, n, p_true) + stats.binom.sf(hi - 1, n, p_true)


def tail_table(ns):
    ns = np.asarray(ns)
    return pd.DataFrame({
        "n": ns,
        "exact": [exact_tail(n) for n in ns],
        "CLT approximation": 2 * stats.norm.sf(eps * np.sqrt(ns) / np.sqrt(p_true * (1 - p_true))),
        "Hoeffding": np.minimum(1, 2 * np.exp(-2 * ns * eps ** 2)),
        "Chebyshev": np.minimum(1, p_true * (1 - p_true) / (ns * eps ** 2)),
    })


print(tail_table([10, 20, 50, 100, 200, 500, 1000]).to_string(index=False, float_format=lambda v: f"{v:.5f}"))



# Figure 3.5 — the probability of a deviation of 0.1: exact value and bounds
def figure_3_5():
    ns = np.arange(10, 1001, 5)
    tab = tail_table(ns)
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.6, 4.2))
    ax.plot(tab["n"], tab["exact"], color="black", linewidth=2.2, label="exact (binomial)")
    ax.plot(tab["n"], tab["CLT approximation"], color=GREEN, linestyle=":", linewidth=2, label="CLT approximation (not a bound)")
    ax.plot(tab["n"], tab["Hoeffding"], color=BLUE, linestyle="--", linewidth=2, label=r"Hoeffding $2e^{-2n\varepsilon^2}$")
    ax.plot(tab["n"], tab["Chebyshev"], color=VERMILION, linestyle="-.", linewidth=2, label=r"Chebyshev $\sigma^2/(n\varepsilon^2)$")
    ax.set_yscale("log")
    ax.set_ylim(1e-12, 2)
    ax.set(xlabel="sample size $n$", ylabel=r"$\mathbb{P}(|\bar X_n - 0.3| \geq 0.1)$",
           title="A deviation of 0.1 for the mean of Bernoulli(0.3) variables")
    ax.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=9.5, loc="lower left")
    fig.tight_layout()
    plt.show()


figure_3_5()



On the logarithmic scale of Figure 3.5 an exponential decay is a straight line. The exact probability (black) decays exponentially, and Hoeffding’s bound (blue dashed) decays at nearly the same exponential rate, staying above the truth by a modest factor: it is a guarantee that is also informative. Chebyshev’s bound (vermilion) decays only polynomially and is useless for large n, though it is better than Hoeffding’s for n up to about 100 in this table, because Hoeffding uses only the range of the variables, while Chebyshev uses their variance (0.21 here, less than the worst case 0.25 of the range [0, 1]). There are sharper inequalities that use both (Bernstein’s, Bennett’s); we do not need them. The Gaussian approximation (green dotted) is the closest to the truth for moderate n, but it carries no guarantee: it is an approximation, not an inequality.

hierarchy.lvl3: Worked example 3.2 — how many coin flips?
hierarchy.lvl2: 3.5 Concentration: from the law of large numbers to Hoeffding’s inequality

records.content:
We want to estimate the probability p that a coin lands heads, to within \varepsilon = 0.05, with confidence 1 - \delta = 0.99. By Hoeffding, it suffices that 2e^{-2n\varepsilon^2} \le \delta, that isn \ge \frac{\ln(2/\delta)}{2\varepsilon^2} = \frac{\ln 200}{2 \cdot 0.0025} = \frac{5.298}{0.005} \approx 1059.7 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad n = 1060.

Chebyshev, in the worst case \sigma^2 = \tfrac14, requires n \ge \frac{1/4}{\varepsilon^2\delta} = 10{,}000. The central limit theorem suggests n \approx (z_{0.995}\,\sigma/\varepsilon)^2 = (2.576 \cdot 0.5/0.05)^2 \approx 664, a number that is right for large n but is not guaranteed. Let us compute the three.

eps_c, delta_c = 0.05, 0.01
n_hoeffding = int(np.ceil(np.log(2 / delta_c) / (2 * eps_c ** 2)))
n_chebyshev = int(np.ceil(0.25 / (eps_c ** 2 * delta_c)))
n_clt = int(np.ceil((stats.norm.ppf(1 - delta_c / 2) * 0.5 / eps_c) ** 2))
print(f"Hoeffding (guaranteed)            : n >= {n_hoeffding}")
print(f"Chebyshev (guaranteed, worst case): n >= {n_chebyshev}")
print(f"CLT (approximate)                 : n >= {n_clt}")

# A sanity check of the Hoeffding sample size by simulation (the worst case is p = 1/2)
rng = np.random.default_rng(SEED)
for n_try in (n_clt, n_hoeffding):
    means = rng.binomial(n_try, 0.5, size=200_000) / n_try
    print(f"n = {n_try:>4}: fraction of 200,000 repetitions with |mean - 0.5| > 0.05: {np.mean(np.abs(means - 0.5) > eps_c):.5f}   (target: at most {delta_c})")



With n = 1060 the failure rate is far below the 1% we allowed: Hoeffding’s guarantee is conservative, because it is valid for every distribution on [0, 1]. The CLT sample size of 664 gives a failure rate close to the nominal 1%, but that holds only because the Gaussian approximation is excellent for a Bernoulli(½) with n \approx 664; for rare events (a probability of 0.01, say) it is much worse.

Key idea

Hoeffding’s inequality is the engine of generalization theory. It turns “the average of n bounded independent variables” into “within \sqrt{\ln(2/\delta)/(2n)} of its mean, with probability at least 1 - \delta”. It requires only independence and boundedness: no Gaussianity, no knowledge of the variance. Its two limitations are the topic of the next sections. It speaks about one function fixed in advance (Section 3.6 handles the function chosen by ERM), and it needs a bounded loss (for the squared loss, one needs other tools, which exist but are beyond this book).

records.content:
Suppose the hypotheses are the classifiers that can be described by 20 binary choices (for instance, 20 yes/no design decisions), so that \lvert\mathcal{H}\rvert = 2^{20} \approx 10^6. How many examples guarantee, with probability 0.99, that every empirical risk is within \varepsilon = 0.05 of the true one?n \ge \frac{20\ln 2 + \ln 200}{2 \cdot 0.05^2} = \frac{13.863 + 5.298}{0.005} \approx 3832.2 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad n = 3833.

To guarantee an estimation error of 0.05 for ERM we need four times as many: n \ge 2 \cdot 19.161/0.0025 \approx 15{,}329, that is n = 15{,}330. Notice the shape of the result: a model that is described by b bits has \ln\lvert\mathcal{H}\rvert = b \ln 2, so the required number of examples grows linearly with the number of bits, and a model with p real parameters stored with 32 bits has at most 2^{32p} different functions, so n grows linearly with the number of parameters p. This is the first appearance of a rule that we will meet again in a sharper form: the number of examples must be larger than the capacity of the model.

def n_uniform(log_h, eps, delta, estimation=False):
    """Sample size from Theorem 3.1 (uniform deviation <= eps) or from Corollary 3.2 (estimation error <= eps)."""
    base = (log_h + np.log(2 / delta)) / (2 * eps ** 2)
    return int(np.ceil(4 * base if estimation else base))


print("|H| = 2^20, eps = 0.05, delta = 0.01")
print("  uniform deviation <= 0.05    :", n_uniform(20 * np.log(2), 0.05, 0.01))
print("  ERM estimation error <= 0.05 :", n_uniform(20 * np.log(2), 0.05, 0.01, estimation=True))
for p_params in (10, 100, 1000):
    print(f"a model with {p_params:>4} parameters of 32 bits: n >= {n_uniform(32 * p_params * np.log(2), 0.05, 0.01):,}")
